profile.name: Sequence dance
profile.tagline: A form of dance where a preset pattern of movements is followed to predetermined music.
profile.insight: Since 1949, the Empress Ballroom in Blackpool, England, has hosted the British Sequence Championships, the most famous annual competition for this style of dance.
profile.profile: Sequence dancing is a form of dance in which a preset pattern of movements is followed, usually to music which is also predetermined. It encompasses various styles, including ballroom, line, square, and circle dances. The practice is both a competitive sport and a social pastime, with roots extending back to the 19th century.
profile.profile_long: Sequence dancing is a form of dance in which a preset pattern of movements is followed, usually to music which is also predetermined. The term encompasses a wide range of styles, including ballroom dances that move around the floor, as well as line, square, and circle dances. Historically, sequence dancing is significantly older than modern ballroom dancing. With the exception of the waltz, which was invented around 1800, all dances performed in ballrooms were sequence dances until the early 20th century. As modern ballroom dancing developed in England, sequence dancing persisted, incorporating 'Old Time' dances alongside adapted versions of new ballroom and Latin dances. Today, the practice functions as both a competitive sport and a social pastime. Modern sequence dancing is characterized by a repeat of steps at every sixteenth bar, typically continuing for five or six sequences in total. Ideally, the music features a four-bar introduction at the correct tempo and rhythm, followed by these sixteen-bar sequences, allowing dancers to progress around the room until the music concludes. There are many different tempo types for sequence dancing, categorized by the specific dance style. These are generally split into three sections: Old Time (also known as Classical), Modern, and Latin, with the dividing line occurring in the early 20th century. New sequences are devised frequently, with over four thousand published as scripts as of 2010. Regular competitions are held between dance teachers to determine which newly created dances are officially adopted and scripted for wider distribution. While most new dances are tried briefly and then archived, a select few gain popularity and become staples of the dance hall, forming the basis of most Tea Dances. Beyond the United Kingdom, the style has evolved into regional variants such as New Vogue, a set of sequence dances developed in Australia in the 1930s that utilizes modern ballroom technique. New Vogue is practiced both socially and competitively across Australia and New Zealand, featuring fifteen competition dances that cover March, Foxtrot, Tango, and Viennese Waltz rhythms. To facilitate the learning and transmission of these dances, a shorthand notation system similar to knitting patterns or text messaging is used. Ultra-keen dancers subscribe to services that distribute these scripts immediately after they are issued by competition organizers. The social aspect of the dance remains vibrant, with dance clubs devoted to the teaching and learning of approved new sequence dances, providing an alternative to the traditional Tea Dance.
